notes.meaning: God speaks to the faithful believers who are earnestly seeking to do what is right. He tells them to look back at their origin, comparing them to stones cut from a single quarry. This reminds them of how their nation began from very humble and small beginnings.

The Lord names the quarry: their ancestors Abraham and Sarah. When God called Abraham, he was only one man with no children, yet God blessed him and turned his family into a great nation. If God could do that before, He can easily multiply and restore the small group of exiles today.

The Lord promises to comfort ruined Jerusalem and show deep compassion on her broken walls. He will transform her dry, empty desert into a lush paradise like the Garden of Eden. The city will once again be filled with joyful songs, thanksgiving, and happy celebrations.

God calls His chosen people to pay close attention to His voice. His teaching and divine justice will go out to reach the entire world like a shining light. His truth is not meant to stay hidden in Israel, but to bring guidance to all nations.

The Lord announces that His rescue and deliverance are coming quickly. His mighty arm will bring fair judgment and rule over the peoples of the world. Even distant lands across the sea will put their hope and trust in His power.

The skies and the ground seem permanent, but they will eventually pass away. The heavens will vanish like smoke, the earth will wear out like old clothing, and mortal people will perish. God's righteousness and salvation, however, will last forever and never fail.

The Lord addresses those who have taken His laws to heart and love to obey them. He tells them not to be afraid when other people mock them or throw insults their way. Believers often face cruel criticism, but God urges them not to be broken by human opinions.

Those who mock God's people are frail and temporary. Just as tiny moth larvae quietly eat away wool until the garment falls apart, human oppressors will soon vanish. In contrast, the Lord's faithful salvation will endure through every generation.

The prophet calls on the Lord to display His mighty power, picturing His arm waking up to act. He points back to ancient history when God crushed Rahab, a poetic nickname for Egypt, and struck down Pharaoh like a dragon. The prayer asks God to perform those same wonders for His people once again.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars note that Rahab and the dragon were ancient poetic symbols for sea monsters representing cosmic chaos, which biblical writers adapted to describe God's defeat of Egypt and pagan powers.

notes.meaning: The prayer recalls the crossing of the Red Sea during the Exodus. God dried up the deep waters to create a safe path for His rescued people to walk across. That historical miracle gives believers confidence that God can deliver them from Babylon as well.

Because of God's power, the ransomed captives will surely return and enter Jerusalem with loud singing. They will be crowned with lasting joy that never ends. All their deep sadness and painful groaning will completely run away.

The Lord Himself answers their plea by promising His personal comfort. He asks why they would ever tremble before mortal men, who quickly wither and die like grass. With the eternal God watching over them, fearing human rulers makes no sense.

By living in constant fear, the exiles had acted as if they forgot the Lord their Maker. He is the very God who spread out the heavens and laid the foundations of the earth. The angry rage of the Babylonian oppressor will soon come to an end and vanish.

The prisoners who are bowed low in chains will soon be set free. They will not starve to death in dark prison pits, because God will make sure they have their daily food. Their long trial in captivity is drawing to a quick close.

The Lord reminds them of His great power over nature. He is the God who commands the raging sea and controls its roaring waves. As the Lord of Hosts, He has entire heavenly armies at His disposal to protect His covenant family.

God places His words into the mouth of His servant and keeps him safe under the protective shadow of His hand. Through this divine work, the Lord is shaping a renewed creation and rebuilding His covenant community. He gives Zion the comforting assurance that they are truly His people.

God calls Jerusalem to wake up and stand on her feet. The city had suffered terrible judgment for her sins, pictured as drinking a cup of divine fury down to its bitter dregs. That punishment had left the nation stunned and stumbling like a drunken person.

Jerusalem is pictured as a dazed mother who is completely unable to walk on her own. None of the sons she gave birth to and raised are able to take her hand and guide her. Her leaders and citizens are too weak to offer her any real help.

A pair of twin disasters hit the nation: ruin and destruction to the land, along with starvation and the sword against the people. Her misery was so immense that no human comforter could be found to console her. Only the Lord could rescue them from such total ruin.

The young men of the city have collapsed from hunger and exhaustion at every street corner. They lie there helpless, like a wild antelope trapped inside a hunter's net. They have felt the full weight of God's rebuke against the nation's past rebellion.

The Lord speaks tenderly to His afflicted city, acknowledging her terrible grief. Her drunkenness did not come from drinking wine, but from the staggering blow of God's heavy discipline. God sees her misery and prepares to speak words of hope.

The Lord God steps in as a defender to plead the cause of His people. He takes the cup of trembling completely out of Jerusalem's hands. He promises that His people will never again have to drink this cup of His wrath.

God hands the cup of judgment over to the cruel Babylonian captors who tormented His people. Ancient conquerors had forced the defeated Israelites to lie flat on the ground so soldiers could walk over their backs. Now those arrogant tormentors will have to face God's justice themselves.
